newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian panel suggests more health care at home.
newsitem.headline: Canadian panel suggests more health care at home.

text.p: A government-appointed panel recommended on Tuesday that Canada should fund more health care at home and provide free prescription drugs in order to cut the country's overall health costs.

The National Forum on Health, appointed by Prime Minister Jean Chretien in 1994, said more funding for homecare would help prevent, delay or substitute more expensive long-term care services, often at hospitals or nursing homes.

Paying for drugs would add to government costs, since they were not covered across the country under the current medicare system. But the panel said total costs might decrease through bulk purchases and controlled pricing.

Federal Health Minister David Dingwall agreed -- though the opposition Reform Party said the drug plan smacked too much of increased government control and the Bloc Quebecois said it would mean federal interference in provincial affairs.
"I'm glad they've recommended the government include homecare and pharmacare (pharmacy costs) in the publicly funded system," Dingwall told reporters after receiving the report.
"It doesn't make much sense that those families that are in need of homecare and those families, those individuals, those seniors that are in need of pharmacare, that they should be excluded."
But he said the federal government could not unilaterally create a national drug plan. It would need the cooperation of the provinces.
"I cannot do it alone but I intend to work with the various stakeholders to make it happen", said Dingwall.

The forum also recommended the government increase funding to the provinces for health and social costs for 1997-98 to $12.5 billion Canadian ($9.1 billion U.S.) to ease the burden on provincial health systems.
This would be an increase of $1.5 billion Canadian ($1.1 billion U.S.) more than budgeted. Finance Minister Paul Martin has slashed spending to try to trim Canada's budget deficit.

Forum Chairman Dr. Tom Noseworthy said Canada's health system was not in crisis but that it was one of the most expensive in the world, costing C$72 billion ($64 billion U.S.) or almost 10 percent of gross domestic product.
"We need to reallocate these resources, to ensure the right dollars are in the right place," he said in a statement.
"In some cases, this could involve reallocating existing funds from private to public spending, and in others by shifting funds from one area of public spending to another."
